Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

finish with distinct information about the planned handoff to the afternoon crew mara intended to ask the next shift to verify the damp chickpea label and take the second cold room reading after the door stayed closed for fifteen minutes the stockroom also had a narrow east aisle that needed to remain clear for the hand cart and a stack of empty crates was already waiting beside the recycling area mention that the Saturday cooking demonstration was expected to use chickpeas carrots and onions but that the final recipe quantity had not been set keep these plans and conditions open and end with the practical detail that the coordinator left the working board visible near the receiving table", "output": "Please prepare a self-contained prompt for a fictional inventory account from the Harbor Table Food Cooperative in a midsized coastal town. The account should focus on one ordinary receiving day in early October, when the cooperative is preparing its weekly member pickup and checking whether the stockroom can support a Saturday cooking demonstration. Ask for a clear, practical narrative rather than a promotional story, and keep the account grounded in the work of staff, volunteers, and members. The requested account should explain what was counted, what was uncertain, and which follow-up steps were planned, without claiming that any unresolved count was settled.

Set the scene in the cooperative's shared warehouse beside its small retail room, and describe how the morning receiving table was arranged before the first delivery arrived. Include the date as October 8 and identify Mara Chen as the inventory coordinator and Leon Price as the volunteer who checked produce deliveries. Mention that two staff members were handling member orders while a driver waited near the loading door. Give the writer room to show routine pressure without suggesting that anyone acted carelessly, and make clear that this is one day's snapshot, not a complete annual audit.

Explain that the cooperative tracks dry goods in sealed cases and loose produce by weight, and that its printed shelf sheet is updated at the end of each shift. The sheet showed 18 cases of chickpeas before receiving, and the new delivery note listed 6 more cases, but one case was left on a hand cart because its outer label was damp. Ask the account to distinguish the written delivery quantity from the quantity that had been physically checked, and to say that the coordinator planned to verify the damp label after the cart was moved away from the aisle.

Include the produce figures as they appeared on the morning board: there were 42 pounds of yellow onions, 27 pounds of carrots, and 16 pounds of spinach. After the first weighing, Leon found that the spinach scale had not been set to zero before the empty tray was placed on it. He repeated the weighing with a clean tray and recorded 14 pounds. Do not state that the first number was erased or that a particular amount was spoiled. Describe the correction as a second measurement, and retain enough detail for a reader to understand why the board and the final count differed.

Ask for a brief account of the cold room as well. The dairy delivery had 9 crates of yogurt and 4 crates of oat milk, and the temperature display read 39 degrees when Mara checked it at 8:20 a.m. The cooperative's routine range was 36 to 40 degrees. She wrote the reading on the daily sheet and said she would look again after the door had been closed for fifteen minutes. Do not turn that planned check into a claim about what the later display showed, and do not imply that the initial reading was outside the stated range.

Explain the records boundary plainly and include the exact instruction “do not modify records.” The account may describe staff comparing the shelf sheet with delivery slips and may mention a proposed note for the next shift, but should not say that anyone changed a signed delivery slip or rewrote the original count. Mara's ordinary spoken comment should appear as a short direct quote. She said, “We counted every crate before lunch, but the east cooler still needs a second check.” Retain the quote as a statement about the count and the pending cooler check, rather than turning it into a guarantee about all stock.

Section One
Ask the writer to follow the flow of the day's work from arrival through the first comparison of paper and physical counts. Start with the chickpea cases and the hand cart, then move to the produce board and the repeat spinach weighing. Explain that Leon put the produce baskets on the blue rack after weighing, and that Mara kept the damp-labeled case separate from the verified cases until its label could be read. Do not invent a supplier name, a replacement delivery, or a decision to reject goods. Show why placing items in separate locations helped staff keep the open question visible.

Include the member pickup context without making it the central subject. The order team had prepared 31 paper bags before receiving began, and three members arrived early to ask whether carrots would be available for a community soup table. Mara checked the board and told them the listed carrot amount was 27 pounds. She did not promise how much would remain after orders were packed. The account should describe that exchange as useful context for inventory planning and should not imply that the members reserved produce or received a special allocation.

Ask for an explanation of the small procedures that kept the count legible. A volunteer wrote units beside each quantity and used pounds for loose produce, while Mara checked case totals against the delivery slips. When a number was uncertain, the team left the earlier entry visible on the working board and placed the new measurement beside it. The account should distinguish that working board from the signed slips and the end-of-shift shelf sheet without suggesting that each document served the same purpose. Avoid adding software systems, barcode scans, or a separate warehouse policy that the cooperative was not said to use.

Finish with distinct information about the planned handoff to the afternoon crew. Mara intended to ask the next shift to verify the damp chickpea label and take the second cold room reading after the door stayed closed for fifteen minutes. The stockroom also had a narrow east aisle that needed to remain clear for the hand cart, and a stack of empty crates was already waiting beside the recycling area. Mention that the Saturday cooking demonstration was expected to use chickpeas, carrots, and onions, but that the final recipe quantity had not been set. Keep these plans and conditions open, and end with the practical detail that the coordinator left the working board visible near the receiving table."}]
